articles.title: Can US midterm election really change Trump's Iran policy?
articles.summary: The US midterms are at hand, but their impact on the Iran war remains far from clear. Analysts say the Washington political elite may not be as divided on Iran as it appears.

image.caption: Trump's Middle Eastern policy played a major role in the midterm election campaignImage: Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images/AFP

blocks.text: The US election this Tuesday is shaping up to be one of the most consequential midterm votes in modern US history, with Washington's relationship with Israel and its war on Iran right at the center of the political standoff.
Many Democrats, including the party's rising stars such as Ohio Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed, are outspoken critics of the Iran war, with El-Sayed calling the conflict "illegal" and "stupid."

US President Donald Trump sought to downplay the effects of the war during the campaign. Last week, he claimed only "one or two targets" remained in Iran and that those could be settled in 10 minutes. However, he immediately added that messages are still being exchanged, Tehran shows strong interest in a deal, and the US has plenty of time to deal with the crisis.

At the same time, there are reports of the US and Israel preparing to launch a new round of strikes on Iran just after the midterm election and pro-war Republicans such as Senator Ted Cruz are putting pressure on the White House to deal with "the threat" posed by Iran.
"I have urged arming the Iranian protesters to overthrow the regime," Cruz said in an online post after spending a day with Trump.

Behind the scenes, analysts warn that the Washington political elite may not be as divided on Iran as it appears. Moreover, even a resounding Democrat victory might not give them enough leverage on the Trump administration regarding the Iran war.
Democrats and Republicans broadly 'in consensus' on Iran

Talking to DW, former National Security Advisor John Bolton said the Democrats are likely to secure a majority in the House of Representatives and possibly the Senate, handing them control of the Iran war funding.
The US Congress "can allocate defense budgets or impose restrictions on the use of financial resources," Bolton said.
Iran conflict: Could a new phase of the war be imminent?
Nevertheless, Bolton points out that the US president can veto congressional legislation, which would then require a two-thirds majority in both assemblies to overcome.
"Even if Democrats hold a majority in both houses, their influence will be limited to the legislative and political tools of Congress," he said.
US diplomat and Iran expert Alan Eyre points to a kind of "bipartisan consensus" that Republicans and Democrats have on Iran.

"Both major US parties share significant common ground in their opposition to the political structure of the Islamic Republic and in their support for policies aimed at exerting pressure on Tehran to change its behavior," he said.
What does Tehran think?
While warning of a "crushing response" to any new strikes on underground sites, Tehran has confirmed ongoing indirect communication via Doha and Muscat, keeping its diplomatic option open.

Shahin Modarres, an international security analyst leading the Iran team at ITSS Verona, told DW that Tehran's actions are based on a miscalculation. The regime, he argues, assumes that a Democratic Congress can easily restrain the White House.

Tehran's strategy in dragging out peace talks, pressuring the Strait of Hormuz, and letting fuel prices weigh on US voters, aims to deny Trump a win before November. However, Modarres notes this strategy may backfire after the election, as the Trump administration will no longer have any reason to delay its moves.
This approach also ignores the fact that both US parties largely agree on not letting Iranian develop nuclear weapons, he said.
How serious are Iran's new threats of retaliation?
Will Trump launch new strikes and declare victory?
Trump's ally-turned-critic John Bolton believes that Trump will only decide on his next steps on Iran after the election, once the political pressure grows less acute.
"I cannot predict what the US President will do; even Trump himself does not know his final decision right now," he told DW.
Bolton cites as an example a possible US attack on "Kuh-e Kolang," the new nuclear site he claims the Iranian government is constructing near Natanz.
"In this scenario, Trump could damage these facilities, declare victory, and pull back."
Bolton: 'Regime change' only guarantee against Iran getting nukes

Trump has consistently emphasized that the US goal is to deny Iran the capability of acquiring nuclear weapons. Throughout the conflict, the US president has also repeatedly claimed his administration had succeeded in this regard.
Bolton, in contrast, believes that the Islamic Republic will continue to pursue nuclear weapons capability for as long as it remains in power.
The former Trump advisor views "regime change" as the only sustainable solution to keep Iran from acquiring nuclear weapons.
US military buildup: What message is it sending Iran?
US failing to communicate with ordinary Iranians

Eyre, the first Persian-speaking diplomat to be the spokesperson for the US Department of State, emphasizes the difficulty of using external tools to bring about sustainable change. In his view, even if there is a consensus in Washington opposing the Islamic Republic and demanding a change in its behavior, this US consensus alone cannot overcome the structural obstacles to political change inside Iran. He reiterates that any fundamental transformation must emerge from within Iranian society itself.
The veteran diplomat also points to the failure of "Washington's public diplomacy to convey a clear, coherent, and authentic message to Iranian society."
He notes that official US government messaging is only incompletely reflected in the media outlets that the vast majority of Iranian citizens rely on for news.
"Furthermore, targeted and principled engagement with the core of Iranian society has generally not been a priority for successive US administrations," he said.
"Iranian citizens see that the US takes certain positions at the rhetorical level, but behaves differently in practice."
According to Eyre, this gap between words and deeds in Washington is a structural phenomenon that is not limited to a single administration or a single election cycle.
Iran's regime: inside the system protecting its rulers

Only 21 out of 24 senator-judges are physically present. articles.title: PLDT’s longtime auditor SGV resigns, withdraws opinion amid accounting issues
articles.summary: PwC takes over the telco giant’s audits after SGV earlier identified a material weakness in financial reporting controls and withdrew its 2024 and 2025 audit opinions

blocks.text: PwC takes over the telco giant’s audits after SGV earlier identified a material weakness in financial reporting controls and withdrew its 2024 and 2025 audit opinions

items: SyCip Gorres Velayo & Co. (SGV) has resigned as PLDT's auditor after nearly 24 years, citing impaired independence under US SEC rules.
SGV withdrew its audit opinions on PLDT's 2024 and 2025 financial statements due to previously uncovered accounting errors and a material weakness in internal controls.
PLDT has appointed Isla Lipana & Co. (PwC) as its new external auditor, while still seeking an auditor for its international financial statements.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – After nearly 24 years of serving as PLDT’s auditor, SyCip Gorres Velayo & Co. (SGV) has resigned and withdrawn its audit opinions on the company’s 2024 and 2025 financial statements prepared for international reporting.

SGV, the country’s largest professional services firm and a member of Ernst & Young, informed PLDT on October 31 that it was resigning after determining that it was no longer independent under US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) and auditing oversight rules.

“SGV has now concluded that its independence was impaired as of the issuance of its Fiscal 2025 Audit Opinions, and this impairment continues through today. Accordingly, SGV has submitted its resignation as the Company’s independent registered public accounting firm,” PLDT said in a disclosure.

An external auditor is supposed to independently examine a company’s financial statements and assure investors that these fairly present its finances. SGV concluded that its independence had already been impaired when it issued its 2025 audit opinions in April. While PLDT’s disclosure discussed the accounting errors and weaknesses in its financial controls, it did not specify what caused SGV’s independence to be impaired.

SGV’s resignation comes after accounting errors were earlier uncovered at PLDT. In August, PLDT acknowledged these errors arising from “deficiencies in controls over the accounting for certain structured hedge arrangements.” These hedge arrangements often protect companies from financial risks, such as fluctations in currency exchange rates. The errors involved how gains and losses from these contracts were recorded in its financial statements.
More seriously, SGV concluded that “a material weakness existed in the Company’s internal control over financial reporting as of December 31, 2025.”
SGV had initially issued unqualified, or clean, audit opinions on PLDT’s 2024 and 2025 financial statements before now withdrawing them following the discovery of accounting issues.

The auditor has since withdrawn its 2025 audit opinions, saying they “could no longer be relied upon.” On October 31, it also withdrew its 2024 opinion because it could not complete its assessment of additional accounting information before resigning.

PLDT said there had been no disagreements with SGV over accounting practices or audit procedures, apart from the unfinished assessment. The telco giant also stressed the revisions identified so far were not expected to materially affect its net income, EBITDA, earnings per share, cash flows, or key operating metrics.

Still, the August disclosure was serious enough for the Philippine Stock Exchange to halt trading in PLDT shares for one hour on August 14 as investors digested the news. PLDT shares later fell 4.49% to P1,170 by the end of that day.

It was not PLDT’s first controversy involving financial controls. In December 2022, the company disclosed capital expenditure budget overruns estimated at P48 billion covering 2019 to 2022. A later review found no evidence of fraud, but PLDT still introduced changes to its spending controls. (READ: PLDT cleans up, moves on from capex overrun mess)
Meanwhile, PLDT appointed Isla Lipana & Co., the Philippine member firm of PwC, as its new external auditor effective Monday, November 2.

PwC will handle its Philippine financial statements, but PLDT is still searching for an auditor to handle its international financial statements and internal control reporting required by US regulators. PLDT’s US reporting obligations arise from its listing on the New York Stock Exchange, where its American depositary shares trade.

PwC Philippines’ chairman emeritus, Alexander Cabrera, recently grabbed the spotlight as the forensic accounting expert who testified for the prosecution in Vice President Sara Duterte’s impeachment trial in October. – Rappler.com

articles.title: US urges Venezuela to release remaining political prisoners
articles.summary: The US secretary of state also discusses laying the groundwork for 'free, fair, and credible elections'.

blocks.text: The US has urged Venezuela to release the remaining political prisoners being held in the South American country.

More than 1,000 political prisoners have been freed since US forces seized Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro in a military raid on Caracas on 3 January and took him to New York, where he faces trial on drug-trafficking and torture charges.
But Venezuelan prisoners' rights group Foro Penal says 322 people remain in detention.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio met his Venezuelan counterpart, Oliver Blanco, on Monday where he called for their release and discussed reforms aimed at laying the groundwork for free, fair, and credible elections, the US state department said.
The release of political prisoners has long been a demand made by Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado.

Machado, who was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 2025, returned to Venezuela on 25 October after living in exile for almost a year. One of her first meetings was with relatives of political detainees.
Many of those in detention were arrested in the aftermath of the 2024 presidential election.

The National Electoral Council (CNE) - which is dominated by government loyalists - declared the incumbent, Nicolás Maduro, the winner of the election even though copies of the voting tallies collected by the opposition and verified by independent media suggested that the opposition candidate had won.
The Carter Center, which had sent independent observers to Venezuela, also said that the election "could not be considered democratic".

A UN fact-finding mission found, external that in the months that followed, the Venezuelan government orchestrated "a harsh repression against persons perceived as political opponents or simply because they express dissent or critical views against the authorities".
After US forces seized Maduro, his loyal vice-president, Delcy Rodríguez, was sworn in as interim president.
While Rodríguez has the backing of the Trump administration, opposition parties within Venezuela have been expressing impatience with the slow pace of reforms.

In Monday's statement, the US state department stressed that it remained committed to US President Donald Trump's three-phase plan, consisting of "stabilisation, economic recovery and political reconciliation, and democratic transition".
A week ago, Rubio had told journalists that Venezuela's "election infrastructure" had to be replaced in order for fresh elections to be valid.
"Not in 10 years, not in five years, not in two years; it needs to happen quickly under the timelines that we've established," he insisted.
Days later, Rodríguez told Venezuelans in a televised address that "there will be elections" under a "renewed" electoral authority.
However, she did not give a timeline for when the election could be held.
Opposition leader Machado, on the other hand, has been pushing for elections to be held in 2027.
At one point she suggested 24 July 2027 - the anniversary of the birth of independence hero Simón Bolivar - but she has since returned to calling for a vote at some point in the next year.

articles.title: Deadly fire at CFB Wainwright renews compliance clash between oil operator and Alberta regulator
articles.summary: Calgary-based Sumerian Oil and Gas is planning legal action against the Alberta Energy Regulator following months of enforcement issues. The company now alleges that its assets on Canadian Forces…

image.caption: The burn area on Canadian Forces Base Wainwright, south of the central Alberta town, on Oct. 19. Military officials say energy infrastructure wasn't involved in the deadly fire, but an oil and gas company says its recently seized wells on the site were not properly shut down before the incident. (Ch

blocks.text: The deadly fire that swept across the Wainwright, Alta., military base has renewed a months-long regulatory battle between the provincial energy regulator and an oil and gas company.

Military officials have said there is no evidence that energy infrastructure was involved in the grass fire at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright on Oct. 17, which killed four soldiers and injured dozens more.

But in the weeks since the tragedy, Calgary-based Sumerian Oil and Gas has been speaking out against the Alberta Energy Regulator (AER) about recent enforcement issues that led to hundreds of Sumerian wells on the military base being seized days before the fire.
In a series of public statements shared on its website and with CBC News, company officials allege that the AER failed to ensure the wells were secured before the fire.

They say Sumerian staff were the first to alert the regulator that night about the risk the wells could pose as the flames spread. As of Tuesday, the company website appeared to have been taken offline.

items: Rapid spread of fire was main factor in CFB Wainwright deaths, injuries: top military commander

blocks.text: Officials with the AER have not responded to questions about the status of Sumerian's wells on or since the night of the training disaster. They also declined to comment on how the wells have been managed since Sumerian lost access and the assets were placed under the care of the Orphan Well Association (OWA) on Oct. 5.
'New compliance issues'
In a statement to CBC News Friday, Lars DePauw, president of OWA, said the agency has secured Sumerian’s wells at CFB Wainwright.
DePauw did not answer questions about when that work was completed or whether it happened before or after the fire.

“All Sumerian wells on CFB Wainwright have been inspected and shut in,” the statement said. “We continue to work on the new compliance issues we have identified. The OWA was not involved in any emergency response activities during the recent fire.”

items: Alberta premier promises new process to clamp down on delinquent oil and gas operators

blocks.text: OWA previously told CBC News that the AER’s Oct. 5 order against Sumerian was due to “significant non-compliance issues.”

While there are operational oil and gas wells scattered across CFB Wainwright, military investigators have said there is no indication that the fire was caused by oil or natural gas infrastructure, or that a gas line was struck. In response to questions about Sumerian’s assets on the base, military officials said there is no new information to share and the investigations remain active.
Call for ministerial review, legal challenge

Sumerian officials assert that the AER has unfairly targeted its operations for months. They have pledged to launch a regulatory appeal and seek a court injunction in an attempt to regain operational control of their assets.
The company has also asked Alberta Energy Minister Brian Jean to launch a ministerial review into the regulator’s conduct. Jean’s office has not responded to repeated requests for comment.

items: Alberta oil and gas company ordered to abandon assets for repeated non-compliance

blocks.text: In a series of statements issued after the Wainwright fire, Sumerian said it lost custody of its wells on the base two weeks earlier and hasn't had access since.
In the AER order on Oct. 5, all of Sumerian’s assets, including more than 300 well licences on CFB Wainwright, were placed under the care of the OWA.
The order followed a string of enforcement actions, unpaid regulatory fees and a pair of crude leaks that allegedly went unaddressed in Wainwright and Killam.

The order required the OWA to shut in the sites within 14 days, a timeline Sumerian officials had warned the regulator was impossible due to the complicated process required to access sites on an active military base.

“So far as Sumerian can determine, between Oct. 5 and Oct. 17 the OWA did not attend a Sumerian site on the range, shut in no well, and isolated no pipeline," the company told CBC News in a statement.
Sumerian officials said they called the OWA emergency line the night of the fire to report that the company's wells were “inside the fire area.”

items: Deadly CFB Wainwright fire started on grenade launcher range firefighters couldn't enter, officials say

blocks.text: “On the evening of Oct. 17, the OWA’s designated contact advised Sumerian that none of the Sumerian wells on the range had been shut in and that the OWA did not plan to attend the base until Oct. 27,” the company said in a statement posted to its website last week and emailed to CBC News.

Military officials have said the fire resulted from a training exercise, was initially reported on the base's grenade-launcher range — a "permanent danger area" that base firefighters couldn't enter — and quickly spread in strong winds.
Three separate investigations are underway, and, among other things, will look at the threat assessment of the fire.

In a statement to CBC News Wednesday, the AER declined to comment on Sumerian’s allegations and said it is unable to answer questions related to the Wainwright incident while it is under investigation.
Mandy Olsgard, a risk assessment specialist and former senior environmental toxicologist with the AER, was critical of Sumerian’s attempts to regain operational control.

items: Minister's strategy for cleaning up Alberta's abandoned oil wells panned, criticized for lack of public input

blocks.text: The AER's order followed well-documented issues that raise legitimate concerns about the adequacy of environmental management under Sumerian, she said.

Rather than invoking a tragedy of unconfirmed cause to undermine the regulator's credibility, Sumerian should provide evidence that outstanding environmental protection obligations have been met, she said.
"They clearly were not managing their wells in a manner that was sufficient for the Alberta Energy Regulator and that's why they no longer have control of them."
Previous sanctions

Sumerian’s regulatory disputes date back to November 2025, when it acquired the assets of Cleo Energy Corp., which had been in receivership for more than a year while its operations racked up a series of enforcement orders.
The AER did not oppose the initial acquisition, but enforcement disputes continued to arise.
The regulator first ordered Sumerian to suspend operations in July, but the company challenged the order and was granted a temporary stay in the Court of King’s Bench.

When announcing the Oct. 5 order, the AER said it had authorized the OWA to suspend the wells and facilities out of concerns Sumerian “may not be able to provide reasonable care and measures” to protect public safety and the environment.
'Licence loss as a last resort'
The company, however, claims it was not given enough time to fix years-old operational issues before the AER clamped down and seized its assets.
Sumerian asserts that the AER violated its own principles of "education first and proportionate enforcement," punishing the operator for pre-existing conditions on unworkable timelines.

items: Approval of sour gas pipeline permit without consultation triggers Alberta court battle over safety setbacks

blocks.text: Sumerian claims the AER repeatedly miscalculated compliance and security obligations by attributing third-party or non-existent assets to Sumerian. Along with the company's call for a ministerial review, Sumerian is also demanding a regulatory audit of their assets.
“The deficiencies pre-date the restructuring, and the AER knew it,” the company said in a public statement about its dealings with the regulator.

“The company’s position is that the enforcement rests on conditions that pre-date its ownership, contradicts the AER’s own documents, and runs against the AER’s published policy of proportionate enforcement with licence loss as a last resort.”
Oil assets 'dotted' across Alberta
Olsgard said the adequacy of Sumerian's environmental management and its ability to meet regulatory obligations should be assessed on their own merits.

She said, however, the case is a reminder of the need for clear emergency management protocols for the thousands of abandoned and orphaned energy sites scattered across Alberta, and the dangers these operations, if left unsecured, could pose when seasonal wildfires spark.

"We are a petro state, and these are dotted all over our province," she said. "And given the increasing intensity and magnitude of forest fires, this should be something our provincial government is looking into.”

articles.title: Defense’s list of witnesses in Sara Duterte trial expected this week
articles.summary: 'We issued an advisory last week which reminded the defense that it should provide the Court with a list of its witnesses at least five days before their intended date of presentation,' says Senate…

blocks.text: VEEP. Vice President Sara Duterte talks to supporters as she prepares to leave the Quezon City Regional Trial Court after the postponement of the arraignment for her grave threats case, on October 9, 2026.
Noel Celis/Reuters

'We issued an advisory last week which reminded the defense that it should provide the Court with a list of its witnesses at least five days before their intended date of presentation,' says Senate Secretary Renato Bantug Jr.

items: The defense counsel for Vice President Sara Duterte is preparing to present evidence in the impeachment trial and is expected to request subpoenas for witnesses this week.
The Senate impeachment court has a five-day rule requiring the defense to submit a list of witnesses before their presentation, and the trial is set to resume on November 9.

The prosecution has withdrawn most articles of impeachment, allowing the defense to focus on rebutting the remaining unexplained wealth case, while the court awaits the defense's formal comments on recent rulings.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – The defense counsel of Vice President Sara Duterte is preparing to present its evidence in the ongoing impeachment trial, with the Senate impeachment court expecting it to seek subpoenas for its witnesses this week.

Senate Secretary and Clerk of Court Renato Bantug Jr. said on Tuesday, November 3, that the defense is expected to request the issuance of subpoenas for its list of witnesses ahead of the resumption of the proceedings.
This is in accordance with the five-day rule of the Senate impeachment court, which requires the defense to submit its list of witnesses at least five days before their intended presentation.

“We issued an advisory last week, which among others, reminded the defense that it should provide the Court with a list of its witnesses at least five days before their intended date of presentation,” Bantug said.

The impeachment trial was temporarily paused to give way for the Senate committee hearings on the proposed 2027 national budget. Trial will resume on Monday, November 9, with the defense beginning its presentation of evidence.
Prior to the break, the prosecution team in the impeachment trial withdrew all but one of the articles of impeachment to expedite the proceedings, a move that the impeachment court accepted.

Senate impeachment court Presiding officer Francis “Chiz” Escudero said the defense team no longer needs to present counter-evidence for all the dropped cases, and can focus on rebutting the prosecution’s unexplained wealth case.

Escudero also lifted the sub judice rule covering the withdrawn articles, but the ruling drew objections from the defense team. The impeachment court said it would await the defense’s formal comment before deciding whether to reconsider the ruling, either in whole or in part.
Bantug said the defense had yet to submit its formal comment on the matter.
In a related development, the Senate impeachment court issued an advisory on the schedule of the trial for November.
The calendar for the trial is as follows:

November 10 — 10:00 am to 6:30 pm
November 11 — 10:00 am
November 12-13 — 10:00 am to 6:30 pm
November 19-20 — 10:00 am to 6:30 pm
November 23— 10:00 am to 2:00 pm

articles.title: Myanmar natives ask CA: Compel DOJ to act on war crimes complaint vs junta
articles.summary: Petitioners invoke universal jurisdiction, a legal concept under which countries are obliged to prosecute grave crimes in the world due to the belief that all nations have equal duties to mankind

blocks.text: FILING. Members of the Chin Human Rights Organization and their lawyers file a petition with the Court of Appeals to compel the Department of Justice to act on their complaint.
Chin Human Rights Organization
Petitioners invoke universal jurisdiction, a legal concept under which countries are obliged to prosecute grave crimes in the world due to the belief that all nations have equal duties to mankind

items: Burmese complainants filed a petition with the Philippine Court of Appeals to compel the Department of Justice to act on their complaint against Myanmar's ruling junta for war crimes.
The complaint, which has been pending for almost three years, alleges atrocities committed by junta forces in the Chin state of Myanmar, including the burning of homes and killings.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – In another bid to seek justice, some Burmese people asked the Philippine Court of Appeals (CA) to compel the local Department of Justice (DOJ) to act on the complaint they filed against Myanmar’s ruling junta.

On Tuesday, November 3, five Chin complainants filed a petition with the CA. They want the appellate court to order the DOJ to docket their almost three-year-old complaint and probe the war crimes allegations against Myanmar’s Senior General Min Aung Hlaing and nine other junta officers.

“The Petition for Mandamus and Certiorari under Rule 65 names Justice Secretary Fredderick A. Vida and Prosecutor General Richard Anthony D. Fadullon as public respondents. It asks the Court to compel them to resolve the motion for reconsideration pending since 11 April 2024 and to docket the complaint, filed under Republic Act No. 9851 (the Philippine Act on Crimes Against International Humanitarian Law, Genocide, and Other Crimes Against Humanity), and conduct a preliminary investigation,” said the petitioners.

On October 25, 2023, the Myanmar natives filed a complaint with the DOJ over the torching of their houses and the killing of their families in the besieged Chin state, located in western Myanmar. The Chin state pushed back against junta forces when the military coup ousted Aung San Suu Kyi in 2021.
But in retaliation, the soldiers went to their place and burned down the town. According to the Chin people, when their natives tried to put out the fire, they were shot and killed.

blocks.caption: Myanmar’s Chin who fled ‘nightmare’ come to Philippines to sue junta for war crimes

blocks.text: As of writing, the Philippine DOJ has yet to docket or formally act on the complaint.

It does not make sense at first to file a complaint in Manila for crimes that allegedly happened in Myanmar. But the petitioners invoked universal jurisdiction, a legal concept under which countries are obliged to prosecute grave crimes in the world due to the belief that all nations have equal duties to mankind.
The complaint is lodged under RA No. 9851, the local law that transformed international criminal law into a domestic law.

The law’s Section 17 states that Philippine “authorities may surrender or extradite suspected or accused persons in the Philippines to the appropriate international court, if any, or to another State pursuant to the applicable extradition laws and treaties.” (READ: PH may surrender suspects to international court, says DOJ)
According to the petitioners, the DOJ refused to act on the complaint because it read this section as requiring the accused to be present in the country.

“Mandatory universal jurisdiction means that when crimes of international concern, such as war crimes, are brought before Philippine prosecutors, the State has a legal duty, not a mere option, to investigate and, where the evidence warrants, prosecute them, whatever the perpetrators’ nationality and wherever they are. The petition traces this duty to the peremptory (jus cogens) prohibition of war crimes, which the Constitution makes part of Philippine law, and to Section 2(e) of the Act,” said the petitioners.

“Section 17(b) speaks of an ‘accused,’ a status acquired only when charges are filed in court; at the preliminary investigation stage, persons are merely respondents. The opening clause of Section 17 covers persons ‘suspected or accused.’ On the DOJ’s reading, the ban on double jeopardy would also protect only foreigners found in the Philippines, an absurd result,” they added.
The petitioners also raised concerns about the delay in resolving their complaint. They also invoked the constitutional right to the speedy disposition of cases and the guarantee of due process.

“The right to the speedy disposition of cases is not a courtesy. It is a guarantee written into Article III, Section 16 of our Constitution. Three years of silence is not neutrality. For a displaced population whose witnesses are aging, every month of delay is prejudice,” said Romel Bagares, co-counsel for the petitioners.
“If Section 17 is robust enough for the State to wield in other cases, it cannot be too weak for these Chin victims to invoke in theirs,” Gilbert Teruel Andres, co-counsel, added. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Football: Spanish player dies on after cardiac arrest on the pitch
articles.summary: Tenerife forward Jesus de Miguel has died following a collision with the opposing goalkeeper. The Spanish second division club has said it is "heartbroken" at the loss.

image.caption: Jesus de Miguel died after a collision during a Spanish second division matchImage: Ivan Sanchez Jimenez/Avalon/IMAGO

blocks.text: "Heartbroken with pain, with a lump in our throat and unable to believe this is real." Those were the words with which Spanish second division football club Tenerife confirmed the death of their 30-year-old player, Jesus de Miguel, on Tuesday.

De Miguel, 30, was involved in a clash in the middle of the pitch with FC Andorra's Equatorial Guinea international goalkeeper Jesus Owono, who had raced out of his goal to try and clear the ball with the score 2-2 late in the game. Owono was sent off and the match was abandoned.

Spanish media said that De Miguel suffered a cardiac arrest and was resuscitated. The player was taken to hospital and placed in intensive care, with Tenerife later saying that De Miguel's condition had "worsened neurologically", before his death.

After confirming the death on Tuesday morning, the club posted that: "No words can ease the pain, nothing can lessen this great feeling of sadness. Our thoughts are with the family, his close friends and Tenerife fans, who today are grieving over this terrible news."
Andorra also sent their "most sincere condolences" as messages of support began to flood in on Tuesday.
"I am so deeply sorry. Rest in peace, Jesus," former Barcelona defender Gerard Pique, Andorra's majority shareholder, wrote on social media.

blocks.caption: Jesus de Miguel joined Tenerife in 2025Image: REUTERS

blocks.text: Real Madrid, Barcelona, Atletico Madrid and other clubs in Spain also sent messages of condolence, as well as the Spanish FA (RFEF).
"Shattered by this sad news, the Royal Spanish Football Federation wishes to express our deepest sorrow at his passing today," wrote the federation in a statement.
The RFEF postponed Tuesday's matches in the Copa del Rey and Copa de la Reina, "as a gesture of respect and solidarity."

De Miguel had been with Tenerife since joining from from Castellon in 2025. He began his career with Leganes at youth level in the Madrid suburbs, playing for a string of teams, including Unionistas de Salamanca, before signing for Castellon in 2023.

articles.title: Indian tourist killed after two helicopters collide near Everest base camp
articles.summary: The two aircraft crashed just metres from the ground after trying to land at the same spot.

blocks.text: An Indian tourist has died after two helicopters collided while attempting to land near the base camp of Mount Everest, two officials have confirmed to the BBC.

Verified footage of the crash showed the helicopter blades of the two aircraft clipping each other as they came into land at around 08:15 local time (02:30 GMT) in Pheriche, approximately 12km (7 miles) south of Mount Everest Base Camp.
Helicopter company Fishtail Air named the man killed in the crash as Vasanth Kumar Balaramudu.
The helicopter company said one of its vehicles was involved in the collision and that another passenger and the helicopter's captain had been injured.
The injured passengers and crew members on board were rescued and taken to Kathmandu, Fishtail Air added in a statement.
The injured passenger was a tourist from New Zealand, an official of Solukhumbu district, Bhupendra Thapa, told BBC Nepal.
The other helicopter involved was operated by Air Dynasty and had been carrying cargo, the company said.
It was operated by one crew member who sustained no injuries, it added.

articles.title: What’s with Marcos’ new EO on class suspensions?
articles.summary: Blanket orders no more? President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.’s Executive Order No. 130 provides an updated framework for declaring #WalangPasok.

blocks.text: Blanket orders no more? President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.’s Executive Order No. 130 provides an updated framework for declaring #WalangPasok.

items: President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. signed Executive Order No. 130, introducing three mechanisms for class suspension.
The goal is to minimize lost instructional time.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
MANILA, Philippines – School heads are now more empowered to suspend and resume classes following a new executive order (EO) from President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.

EO No. 130, signed last Wednesday, October 28, and publicized on Tuesday, November 3, introduces a framework for the suspension and resumption of face-to-face classes through the following mechanisms: automatic, localized, and granular.
The EO also seeks to ensure the “uninterrupted delivery of quality education through risk-informed, science-based, locally responsive policies that support learning continuity.”
Pending formal implementing guidelines, which must be issued within 30 days, let’s try to break down this new EO.
Through granular suspensions, a school can suspend classes even if there is no applicable automatic suspension or localized suspension ordered by a local chief executive.
This must be based on the determination of actual or imminent threat to the safety, health, and welfare of students and school personnel over “documented site-specific conditions.”

School heads can also declare resumption of face-to-face classes earlier than the prescribed end of the localized suspension. For this, school assessments must show that the “conditions warranting suspension no longer exist or have been sufficiently mitigated” to ensure safety of students and personnel.
The granular suspension and resumption of classes must still be in coordination with the local chief executive.

Automatic suspension is based on the warnings, advisories, alert levels, forecasts, or other issuances from agencies such as the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical, and Astronomical Services Administration or PAGASA; the Philippine Institute of Volcanology and Seismology or Phivolcs; and the Environmental Management Bureau.
The EO states that “suspension shall automatically take effect, without need of further declaration.”
The thresholds for the warnings and other issuances must be specified in the implementing guidelines.

An example for this could be Pasig City’s class suspension guidelines, which list various scenarios during emergencies, not only wind signals for tropical cyclones, where automatic suspensions will apply.

Face-to-face classes will automatically resume once the warnings or other issuances have been “lifted, downgraded, expired, or ceased,” and the required safety assessment inspections have been completed.

When there is no applicable automatic suspension, local chief executives may declare localized suspension “within specific areas in their jurisdiction” based on documented local risk assessments and prevailing conditions.
According to the EO, the local chief executive must specify the following:

items: Areas covered by the suspension, which may include an entire locality or specific places or barangays
Schools covered, as far as practicable
Duration of the suspension

blocks.text: The local chief executive should consult barangay captains, schools division superintendents, and heads of private schools for the scope and duration of the class suspension.
Classes will resume once the period specified in the suspension order ends, and safety assessment inspections are completed.
The Department of Education (DepEd) proposed these revised guidelines on class suspensions to Malacañang in September, in a bid to amend EO No. 66, which was signed in 2012.
The new EO comes months after the DepEd updated its own class suspension guidelines to adopt the 4H framework, or Hayo (Continue), Hinay (Ease-in), Hinga (Check-in), and Hinto (Stop).
The 4H framework guides schools on what learning mode to use in specific emergencies. It also introduced the concept of granular or school-based suspension orders.

“While learner and teacher safety remains strictly non-negotiable, we can no longer rely on sweeping, blanket suspensions when a campus is dry, safe, and ready to teach,” Education Secretary Sonny Angara said in a statement on Tuesday.

“By authorizing granular resumptions alongside localized suspensions, President Marcos is giving our school heads and local executives the legal framework to reopen cleared campuses safely without waiting for broader declarations.”
Since 2024, the Second Congressional Commission on Education (EDCOM 2) has pushed for the policy shift as it found significant class time lost to calamity-related suspensions.
Particularly, it found that schools lost an average of 15 school days annually due to calamity-related suspensions in the past two school years.

“While our learners’ safety remains the priority, we also have to recognize that every day of lost instruction has consequences, particularly for children who are still learning how to read. We cannot allow the worsening of learning loss because of blanket suspensions that could have been more granular and targeted,” EDCOM 2 Commissioner and Senate President Win Gatchalian said.
The guidelines on the suspension and resumption of classes will be tested in the coming months as the country experiences the effects of El Niño. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Norway joins Finland in boycotting hockey world championship games against Russia
articles.summary: Norway joined Finland in pledging to boycott games against Russia at the ice hockey world championship as a rift in the sport deepened Tuesday.

blocks.text: Hockey·New
Norway joined Finland in pledging to boycott games against Russia at the ice hockey world championship as a rift in the sport deepened Tuesday.
Court of Arbitration for Sport ruled last week that the IIHF must reinstate Russian teams
· The Associated Press
· Posted: Nov 03, 2026 6:49 AM EST | Last Updated: 9 minutes ago
Russia is back in the hockey world champions | Hanomansing Live

The Court of Arbitration for Sport ruled last week that the International Ice Hockey Federation must reinstate Russian teams, beginning with the world juniors starting next month in Canada. Finland announced Monday it is rallying other nations to boycott games against Russia.

“Our position is that Russia should be excluded from all international championships as long as the war in Ukraine continues and remains unchanged,” the Norwegian Ice Hockey Association said in a statement. “At the same time, this decision is based on our responsibility to protect the safety and wellbeing of our players, team staff and their families. We believe that playing Russia under the current circumstances could expose our players and team staff to significant security risks. Our priority is therefore their health, wellbeing and personal safety.”

Norway only referred to the men's world championship in May in its statement and said its team would play other games in the tournament. It was not immediately clear if the decision also applies to world juniors.
Finland is the defending men's world champion and Norway was the bronze medal-winner this year.

items: Finland says its national teams won't play against Russia in hockey tournaments
Russia is back in the hockey world championships after sports court ruling

blocks.text: Norway joining the boycott means that at least one team in each of the two groups has now pledged not to play Russia. Reports in Latvian media have indicated Latvia could refuse to play Russia as well.
Germany could pull out of hosting the men's world championship next year over concerns about costs and security, while a longtime tournament sponsor has demanded its logo no longer be shown.
Junior tournaments are affected too, with the Finnish city of Turku saying it will not co-host next year's world juniors if Russia participates.
The Czech government could bar Russian players entry for the women's under-18 world championship there in January.
The women's world championship starting in Denmark this week is not affected by the CAS ruling and is going ahead without Russia.

articles.title: Asian Cup postponed due to Middle East conflict
articles.summary: The Asian Cup has become the latest sporting event to be affected by the ongoing conflict in the Middle East. Organizers cite "exceptional circumstances" in Saudi Arabia, which has seen several…

image.caption: Even during the last month's Gulf Cup there was speculation about a postponement of the Asian CupImage: Ibraheem Abu Mustafa/REUTERS

blocks.text: A little over two months before it was set to kick off, the Asian Football Confederation (AFC) has postponed its flagship international football tournament in the wake of recent deadly attacks on host country, Saudi Arabia.
The AFC cited "substantial logistical complexities and travel disruptions" caused by conflicts in the region.

Instead of January 7, 2027, the tournament will now kick off on December 23 and end on January 21, 2028. The postponement follows delays and cancellations of a number of sporting events in the region, including a Formula One race, the men's and women's tennis finals, the 2027 Dakar Rally and disruption to Asia's marquee continental club football tournament, the AFC Champions League Elite.
Saudi Arabia hosted, and won, the Gulf Cup last month, but there had already been much talk about whether the much larger Asian Cup could go ahead.
Houthi attacks make tournament impossible

It was scheduled to feature 24 teams playing matches in eight venues across Riyadh, Jeddah and Khobar. However, the AFC said that "circumstances arising from developments in the region, including substantial logistical complexities and travel disruptions," made the tournament impossible.

"Exceptional circumstances have been created for the organization and delivery of the competition as originally scheduled, making the postponement necessary in the interest of all participating teams, officials, spectators and other stakeholders."

In particular, the postponement was forced by a recent wave of deadly attacks on Saudi Arabia by Iran-backed Houthi rebels as well as other raging conflicts in the region. The Houthis have targeted Saudi infrastructure, including airports. They are fighting a Saudi-led coalition supporting Yemen's internationally recognized government, a civil war that reignited in July following a years-long truce.
More fighting between Yemen's Houthis, Saudi Arabia
The AFC had been under pressure from several federations to postpone the tournament, with South Korea's players leading the way.
Player and fan safety comes first

"The ongoing military tensions and security instability in the Middle East are issues that cannot be taken lightly," Lee Keun-ho, president of the Korea Professional Footballers Association, said last month, according to the Yonhap News Agency.
Lee added that "no tournament's value can take precedence over the lives and safety of players and football fans."

It seems that the AFC now agrees. However, following the announcement of the postponement, Yasser al-Misehal, chairman of the local organizing committee, promised that Saudi Arabia was "fully ready" whenever the tournament ended up being held.

blocks.caption: The draw for the Asian Cup had been held with great fanfare last May, now the tournament has been postponed for almost a yearImage: Fayez Nureldine/AFP

blocks.text: "The tournament will move to the new dates, and our preparations will continue as planned," he told the Saudi Press Agency.
"We're working closely with the AFC and all our partners to make sure the tournament runs smoothly and meets the high standards expected of Saudi Arabia and the Asian Cup."
Saudi sports investments dwindling with World Cup on horizon

Saudi Arabia has invested hugely in sports over the last decade, from owning Premier League teams to hosting boxing title fights and bidding for a number of major sporting events, most notably World Cup 2034, which they won the right to host unopposed.
However, the country has recently withdrawn or slashed funding for a number of sporting events including golf, rugby, tennis and winter sports.

articles.title: New company wants to stop northern permafrost slumps with special blanket
articles.summary: PermaC Land & Environment Inc. was co-founded by academic and entrepreneur Cansu Culha and former Tetlit Gwich’in chief James Ross. The two incorporated the company in January, and spent the summer…

image.caption: A new company says it has a strategy for stopping retrogressive thaw slumps from growing. It covered a slump near Fort McPherson, N.W.T. this summer with a blanket of wooded fibres and other erosion control materials, and says the test had positive results. (Cristobal Ruiz/Pachamama)

blocks.text: North

PermaC Land & Environment Inc. was co-founded by academic and entrepreneur Cansu Culha and former Tetlit Gwich’in chief James Ross. The two incorporated the company in January, and spent the summer putting their product — dubbed the “green blanket” — to the test.
Business co-founded by entrepreneur Cansu Culha and former Tetlit Gwich’in chief James Ross
A new company that wants to stop permafrost slumps from further erosion says it’s growing its business after testing its product near Fort McPherson, N.W.T., this past summer.

Former Tetlit Gwich’in chief James Ross and academic and entrepreneur Cansu Culha are co-founders of PermaC Land and Environment Inc. The company was incorporated in January and the team spent the summer putting their product — dubbed the “green blanket” — to the test.

“We went out and did the work and learned a lot,” said Ross, who describes the green blanket as a profitable way of healing the land. “Now I have a scientifically proven model of how we can effectively slow down and help these slumps.”

The green blanket is made of biodegradable material that’s laid on top of a retrogressive thaw slump — a kind of landslide that happens when permafrost thaws. The idea is it traps cold in the ground and prevents heat from getting in, while also using a layer of seeds and cuttings to bring back native plants, to try and prevent the gouge in the ground from getting bigger.
James Ross, left, and Cansu Culha co-founded PermaC. They incorporated the company in January and have filed a patent together for their green blanket product. (Cristobal Ruiz/Pachamama)

Culha, who is an adjunct professor at the University of British Columbia, wouldn’t say what, exactly, the blanket was made of saying she had to protect the intellectual property of her company. However, she described it as being made of “wooded fibres” and other erosion control materials.
And, she said, testing it out this summer was a success.

Culha said her team deployed the green blanket on two retrogressive thaw slumps — one stable, the other growing — around 50 kilometres down the Dempster Highway from Fort McPherson in June. The stable slump demonstrated the green blanket did not trigger erosion itself, she said.

The other slump was partially covered to compare the difference between the two sides. Culha said the part of the slump that wasn’t covered retreated five metres, while the land that was covered stayed intact. At the edge of the blanket the land retreated less than one metre, something Culha said was expected because the land next to it was still eroding and exposed the side of the protected area to warm air.
Culha helps deploy her green blanket product on a retrogressive thaw slump near Fort McPherson, N.W.T. this past summer. (Cristobal Ruiz/Pachamama)
Culha said a critical part of her solution is also reintroducing the “very protective” tundra vegetation.

“We believe that the long-term solution is not necessarily to control erosion through these fibres, through these blankets. But rather, it's to bring in native plants that can naturally do the restoration of the lands.”
The problem

Steve Kokelj is a senior permafrost scientist at the Northwest Territories Geological Survey. Not only has he long studied the slump where PermaC has deployed its green blanket, but the company has consulted him on the project as well.
He says permafrost has different characteristics or personality, depending on its history.
The Peel Plateau — where the product was tested — consists of permafrost that’s made up of leftover glacier, and is sometimes made up of 70 to 80 per cent ice, he said.
That’s why when it thaws, the land slumps and settles.

Culha said the green blanket was deployed on part of a retrogressive thaw slump. The part that was left uncovered retreated by five metres, while the part that was covered remained intact. (Cristobal Ruiz/Pachamama)

“A retrogressive thaw slump … they basically start to grow relatively small, when some sort of small erosion or a small landslide exposes the ice and the permafrost, and then that ice thaws in the summertime and the disturbance grows over time.”
Kokelj said a retrogressive thaw slump can “live” and continue to grow for decades.
They can dump huge amounts of sediment into rivers and lakes. Ross said they also pose a risk to infrastructure, and harvesters who travel the land as well.

David Kay, a Gwich’in harvester and sub-chief of the Tetlit Gwich’in Band Council, has seen evidence of this first-hand. Travelling through the mountains, he said he’s seen a lot of erosion alongside creeks and all over the land.
Though he hasn’t had any close calls himself, he’s heard of harvesters chasing animals by snowmobile who have narrowly avoided the steep drop of a slump that’s hard to see.
‘A prudent idea’
Culha said the intent of the green blanket is to stop that positive feedback loop that allows slumps to grow.

“By protecting these slumps from growing further we’re protecting the infrastructure, we’re protecting the streams, the eco-system, as well as preventing the release of carbon, greenhouse gases such as methane, and CO2,” she explained.

Steve Kokelj is a senior permafrost scientist at the Northwest Territories Geological Survey. Not only has he long studied the slump where PermaC has deployed its green blanket, but the company has consulted him on the project as well. (Liny Lamberink/CBC)
In a warming North, Kokelj said the green blanket is a strategy worth pursuing.

“The idea of an insulative blanket is, you know, it seems like a prudent idea. I think coupling that with other things like managing snow, managing drainage, I mean, these are all sort of innovations and ideas that we're going to have to use,” he said.
However, the size of the slump upon which it's deployed will make a difference, he said.

He said it would not be possible to stop erosion of a thaw slump that’s already displaced millions of cubic metres of material. Where there’s likely to be success, he said, is on small disturbances that are just getting started.

Culha said the blanket was deployed in two spots outside of Fort McPherson, N.W.T. One was a stable retrogressive thaw slump, and the other was a slump that had been growing summer after summer. (Cristobal Ruiz/Pachamama)
Kay described PermaC’s solution like a band-aid on the land. He’d like to see the green blanket deployed broadly on Gwich’in lands.
“The land that we have out there is, you know, really unique and beautiful,” he said. “I really think this PermaC company is gonna help us heal the land … I hope it goes a long way.”
Culha wouldn’t say whether PermaC had clients yet. She said the company’s next steps are to think about commercialization and to grow its team.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Liny Lamberink is a reporter for CBC North, covering the Northwest Territories, Nunavut, and Yukon. She moved to Yellowknife in March 2021, after working as a reporter and newscaster in Ontario for five years. You can reach her at liny.lamberink@cbc.ca

articles.title: ‘I am deeply sorry’: Craig Silvey pens 9,000-word apology for child exploitation material offences
articles.summary:
The children’s author claims he experienced trauma in childhood as he begins seven-month sentence for possessing depraved material

  • Warning: This article…

blocks.text: The disgraced best-selling author Craig Silvey has claimed he experienced trauma as a child in a 9,000-word apology published after he was jailed for child exploitation offences.

The young adult novelist was sentenced on Monday to seven months’ imprisonment, after being charged in January and subsequently pleading guilty to distributing and possessing depraved child exploitation material.
The 44-year-old writer posted an article on his Substack titled “My Apology”.
He said that throughout his life he had always been able to find the right words, “but articulating the depth of my contrition and the enormity of my remorse feels beyond my aptitude for language”.
“I am guilty of these offences. I am appalled and mortified by my conduct, and I am deeply, profoundly sorry,” he wrote.
“I want to acknowledge that my engagement with this material is reprehensible and indefensible.
“It is re-traumatising to victims, and perpetuates a cycle of harm.”

Silvey, a father of three, said he betrayed the trust of thousands of people across the country, including those who had read his books, many of whom reacted to his offending with “shock, dismay, disgust, concern and disappointment”.

“I am painfully aware of the possible assumption that my offence must have been informed by a horrible and inappropriate attraction, and that my behaviour must then be connected to sinister and ulterior motivations,” he wrote.
“I assure you this is not the case at all.”
Silvey said he had carried a history of “trauma, shame and anxiety” through most of his life.
Silvey said he suffered a “crisis of mental health and a destructive, despairing breakdown” before he offended.
He was found with numerous sexually explicit photos and videos of children and adults on his laptop and mobile phone when police raided his home in Fremantle.

He also engaged in an online conversation with a person he believed shared his interest in child exploitation material, telling them he preferred boys older than five before adding that “eight was the perfect age”.
“I want to make out with little ones,” the author said in one message.
“I haven’t had any experience, I’m sad to say.
“I’m a bit obsessed.”

Silvey, who has been shortlisted for the Miles Franklin literary award and the International Dublin literary award, is best known for his 2009 coming‑of‑age novel Jasper Jones, which had been considered a modern Australian classic and was adapted into a feature film and several stage productions.
He has also been widely recognised for other books, including Rhubarb, Honeybee – which won the Australian Indie Book Award in 2021 – and the children’s novel Runt, which was also made into a film.

articles.title: Could the AI boom make borrowing more expensive in Europe?
articles.summary: France, Germany and Italy face a volatile bond market as war inflation bites. With US tech giants now issuing billions in AI bonds, they are competing with cash-strapped European governments.

image.caption: AI giants are investing mind-boggling sums in new data centers; those billions are still risingImage: Davide Bonaldo/SOPA Images/Sipa USA/picture alliance

blocks.text: With more than $1 trillion (€900 billion) pouring into the artificial intelligence (AI) build-out, US tech giants are now competing with governments and companies in Europe for the same investment capital.

Four of the Big Five hyperscalers — Amazon, Google-owner Alphabet, Meta and Oracle — have issued around $250 billion in bonds in dollars since the beginning of 2025, according to a tally of filings to US financial regulators by AI Industry Reviews, an independent platform that evaluates AI tools. They have sold a further €37 billion ($41 billion) of bonds in euros.
Recently, Microsoft, the last of the Big Five to hold back, joined the AI borrowing spree with a $25 billion bond sale, all in dollars.
Next year, Goldman Sachs projects that total new AI hyperscaler bond sales are expected to reach $420 billion. About €60 billion will be issued in euros, according to Dutch bank ING.
Battle for investor capital heats up
That is unwelcome news for European companies and countries like France, Germany and Italy, whose sovereign bond yields have risen sharply in recent months and are already straining public finances.

With public debt at 119% of gross domestic product (GDP) and a deficit still running above 5%, France is already paying a sizable risk premium on its debt. Over the past six months, yields on French 10-year bonds have climbed from roughly 3.7% to nearly 5%.
The French government's interest bill is set to rise from €79 billion currently to €91 billion next year and over €100 billion by 2028.
Based on these figures alone, France's Finance Ministry needs to find tens of billions of euros in additional cuts, tax hikes, or more borrowing by the end of the decade.
Could France's debt crisis spread across Europe?

In August, economists at the European Central Bank said the euro bond market was adapting well to the presence of AI giants but warned they "could make it harder for other companies and other economic sectors to access finance."

Writing in a blog post, they also questioned whether the bloc's financial markets can "smoothly handle such large and concentrated debt inflows and warned of a "potential spillover to the sovereign and supranational segment of the bond market."
That means governments and international lenders such as the European Union and the European Investment Bank could also end up paying more to borrow.

blocks.caption: AI data centers cost billions and their energy use is putting pressure on power gridsImage: Jordi Boixareu/ZUMA/picture alliance

blocks.text: 'Bond abundance' helps drive up yields
Viktor Hjort, global head of credit strategy at the French bank BNP Paribas, described the phenomenon as "bond abundance."

Hjort told DW that the presence of the hyperscalers in the euro bond market is "already high enough to create competition" within the corporate sector and "between corporates and governments for available fixed income funds." These are investment funds that mostly buy bonds, which pay regular interest.

Bond yields jumped again last month, driven by rebounding energy prices linked to the Iran war and France’s political crisis, which Hjort said further revealed the growing competition for capital, as government and company borrowing costs rose together.
Normally, nervous investors move into government bonds during uncertain times, which pushes their borrowing costs down.
AI is much hyped, frequently feared, and possibly overrated
European companies could also feel more pain

Goldman Sachs warned last week that rising interest costs were starting to hurt earnings at European companies. Among firms in the Stoxx 600 — an index of 600 large, mid-sized and small companies across Europe — Goldman found that interest costs as a share of sales have risen by nearly half since 2022.
The bank's analysts said this had cut earnings by more than 5% over the same period.

Factor in the competition from AI bonds, and European firms could now face pressure to cut their investments in new plants, equipment and research, as well as shareholder payouts, to prioritize loan repayments.
Regional governments paying the price for AI
The pressure doesn't stop at national governments. Europe's cities and regions, whose borrowing helps to fund schools, transport and infrastructure, may also feel the effects of the AI boom.

A study for the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development(OECD), published in January, compared local bond markets in Belgium, Germany, Spain, Sweden and Canada. Where AI was spreading fastest, measured by the share of AI-related job vacancies, borrowing costs for cities and regions tended to rise.

"Whereas in the United States, my research has found that AI investments are linked to a lower cost of borrowing for municipalities, the opposite appears to hold in several European countries," the study's co-author, Christos Makridis of Arizona State University's W. P. Carey School of Business, told DW.

While AI bonds are far from the sole cause of Europe's widening fiscal strains, US Big Tech's huge appetite for capital could add further pressure next year, due to the additional billions in new bonds planned.
The irony is that European taxpayers could end up paying more on their own governments' debt, partly to help finance an AI boom across the Atlantic.

articles.title: Sherwin Gatchalian: Senate to cut P8.836B in unsupported infra projects
articles.summary: Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian on Tuesday said the Senate would remove infrastructure projects worth P8.836 billion from the proposed 2027 national budget because of missing documentation from…

blocks.text: PROPOSED 2027 NAT'L BUDGET
Published November 3, 2026 6:14pm

Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian on Tuesday said the Senate would remove infrastructure projects worth P8.836 billion from the proposed 2027 national budget because of missing documentation from the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH).
In a statement, Gatchalian said the move followed the disclosure by former DPWH Secretary Vince Dizon that 295 projects had been found to be “non-compliant” in the agency's evaluation.
The evaluation came after Gatchalian flagged eight types of budgetary “red flags” during the DPWH's Senate budget hearing in September.
Gatchalian said more than 62% of the 11,395 infrastructure projects, or 7,107 in total, had at least one major budgetary red flag.
These included projects lacking station numbers and geographical coordinates, lump-sum allocations, overlapping or fragmented projects, and projects with conflicting types of work.

"The Senate is committed unequivocally in weeding out unsubstantiated line items, including those lacking concrete and verifiable technical support, to ensure that every item in the final version is shovel-ready. Unverifiable line items will not receive a single peso of public funding," Gatchalian said.
He said that the Senate would not allocate public funds to projects lacking the necessary supporting documents, saying every peso must be accounted for amid the country's sluggish economic growth.

"Malinaw ang mandato ng Senado, kung walang kaukulang dokumento, walang pondo. Kailangan nating siguruhin na walang puwang ang pang-aabuso sa kaban ng bayan lalo na ngayong mahina ang usad ng ekonomiya at importante ang bawat piso para pasiglahin muli ito," he added.

(The Senate’s mandate is clear: If there are no supporting documents, there will be no funding. We will ensure that there is no room for the abuse of public funds, especially now that the economy is growing slowly and every peso is important in reviving it.)
The People's Budget Coalition (PBC) has flagged more than P1 trillion in potential budgetary “red flags” in the proposed P7.2-trillion national budget for 2027.
PBC co-convenor AJ Montesa said P210 billion in the proposed budget constituted “soft pork” in the form of patronage-driven financial assistance.
Another P695 billion was classified as “hard pork,” consisting of politicized infrastructure projects, while P112 billion was identified as “shadow pork,” or unprogrammed appropriations.

Senate finance committee chairperson JV Ejercito earlier committed to inviting civil society organizations (CSOs) to observe the bicameral conference committee deliberations on the proposed P7.2-trillion national budget.

Meanwhile, Senator Panfilo Lacson said the Senate majority bloc supported efforts to remove questionable allocations from the proposed 2027 budget and ensure transparency in the budget-making process.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: Jet may have broken apart before Florida crash, officials say, as family named among victims
articles.summary: Adam Robinson, Helen Sharp, and their two children - Emma, four, and Charlie, two - died after the plane nosedived.
articles.byline: Nardine Saad, Kathryn Armstrong, Rachel Flynn

blocks.text: Investigators believe parts of a private jet which crashed in Florida and killed all nine on board may have broken off in the air.
The Learjet 60 was bound for the Bahamas from Austin, Texas when it nosedived into a multi-lane highway and exploded on impact.
A tech entrepreneur and his young family, as well as the 20-year-old copilot, were among those who died on Sunday.

The US National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) said weather conditions would be a major focus of the investigation, but that it was struggling to access the wreckage due to a huge crater on the road which was formed by the jet in Palm Beach.
The plane crashed on Military Trail, a six-lane road that features businesses and restaurants, at around 12:50 local time.
"The biggest obstacle that we're going to have is recovering the major wreckage from the impacted crater on the roadway," lead investigator Tim Monville said at a news conference on Monday.

The NTSB said the crater, near the entrance to a mobile home park, was partially filled with water because of severe storms. Heavy rainfall and thunderstorms had been reported in the area at the time of the crash.
Debris was scattered across sports fields, businesses and homes in the area.
"We do have some evidence that there was some breakup of the aircraft before impact," the NTSB's Tom Chapman said.
"We may find parts of the aircraft some distance away from the actual impact site."
Officials are also trying to find out whether a cockpit voice recorder was on board at the time of the crash and if it can be recovered.
Flight analysis indicates that the jet was plummeting hundreds of feet per second before crashing.
In air traffic control audio recordings, someone in the cockpit can be heard reporting "moderate turbulence" and that the crew was "managing the ice".
They can then be heard saying the plane was "picking up precipitation" and "we need to climb". Moments later, the same voice said the plane was descending at a rate of 10,000ft (3,048m) per minute.
An emergency was declared and they can be heard yelling "we are in an overspeed condition descending 20,000ft per minute", before saying, "we are going to crash into the ground".

Seven passengers died on board the flight - named in a joint statement as tech entrepreneur Adam Robinson, his wife Helen Sharp, and their two children - Emma, four, and Charlie, two - as well as Rachael Reed, Charmi Fehr and Anita Maria Cetina.
The pilot was named in media reports as Jeffery Gregory, while Nathalia Filgueiras, 20, who earned her pilot's licence when she was 17, was reported to be the copilot.
One man in a car on the ground sustained a leg injury.
Nathalia Filgueiras's mother, Camila Corteleti, confirmed to US media that her daughter had died in the fireball.
Corteleti told the New York Times: "She loved the freedom. It was completely different seeing the world from the top."
In a 2023 interview with a local news affiliate of CBS News, Filgueiras spoke proudly of receiving her pilot's licence while still a senior in high school.
"I like being different than everyone," she said. "Some people think that it's weird that I can fly planes, but I can't drive a car, I mean I can but, a lot of people think it's funny."

A spokesperson for East Coast Jets, where pilot Jeff Gregory used to work, said: "We are deeply saddened to learn that Capt Jeff Gregory was among those who lost their lives in yesterday's tragic aviation accident in Palm Beach."

articles.title: Sara Duterte defense challenges prosecution evidence in impeachment trial
articles.summary: Vice President Sara Duterte"s defense panel has questioned the admissibility of evidence presented by the prosecution in her impeachment trial, arguing that the documents were neither cited in the…

blocks.text: Vice President Sara Duterte’s defense panel has questioned the admissibility of evidence presented by the prosecution in her impeachment trial, arguing that the documents were neither cited in the Articles of Impeachment nor attached to the original complaints.

In a comment signed by lawyer Karol Grace Oroceo, the defense said the Statements of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth (SALNs) obtained from the Office of the Ombudsman were inadmissible because they were not part of or attached to the impeachment complaints filed before the House of Representatives.

“The 2007-2021 SALNs are inadmissible for lack of relevance to the charges stated in the Articles of Impeachment, as they pertain to a period prior to Respondent’s term as an impeachable officer, without any established connection to the alleged impeachment acts,” the comment stated.
The comment was submitted and received on Oct. 20.

The defense is challenging the admissibility of evidence presented in connection with Article II, the sole remaining charge in the impeachment trial, which accuses Duterte of amassing unexplained wealth disproportionate to her lawful income.
It also accuses her of failing to fully and truthfully disclose her and her husband's assets in their SALNs and of failing to divest from business interests while serving as vice president.
Based on her SALNs, Duterte's declared net worth rose from P7.25 million in 2007, when she entered public office, to P98.656 million in 2025. She was elected as vice president in 2022.
The defense also challenged the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) records, which the prosecution used to show Duterte's alleged financial interests in various companies.

The vice president's defense team argued that the SEC documents covered periods before Duterte became vice president, contained information about corporations unrelated to her, and were supposedly being used to draw mere legal conclusions.

The panel likewise questioned the certification from the Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA) and the Certificate of Marriage of Duterte and her husband, Manases Carpio, saying the documents were not authenticated by a witness and were not attached to the impeachment complaints.

The defense also challenged records from the Philippine Government Electronic Procurement System (PhilGEPS), which the prosecution had presented to establish business transactions involving companies allegedly linked to Duterte. It described the claims drawn from these records as based on “conjectures and assumptions.”

Duterte's lawyers also disputed the “total value” of firearms allegedly owned by the couple, as reflected in Philippine National Police-Firearms and Explosives Office (PNP-FEO) records, which the prosecution cited as personal properties not declared in Duterte's SALNs. The defense said the valuation was unsupported by evidence or testimony from a competent witness.

The defense further questioned the Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC) records and reports concerning alleged substantial transfers and remittances from China, drug trafficking and related offenses, saying these lacked evidentiary support or testimony from a competent witness.
It also argued that the bank records were inadmissible because they had been obtained through a “fishing expedition” and had no clear, direct and substantial connection to Article II.

The defense also challenged the Insurance and Investment Company records, which the prosecution presented to show Duterte's alleged investments, as well as the forensic examination report and related electronic documents, arguing that these were based on mere “assumptions or conjectures” without evidentiary support.
It also questioned the Bureau of Internal Revenue (BIR) records, claiming that the Articles of Impeachment contained no specific allegations related to the documents.
In its comment, the defense said the prosecution had also failed to individually identify and authenticate the companies allegedly linked to Duterte.

In disputing the allegations of conflict of interest, the defense pointed out that Duterte had no business interests in Gencorp Industries Inc. during her tenure as vice president and had no affiliation with the Davao City local government unit, PhilHealth Region X or the Overseas Workers Welfare Administration Region IX.

The defense also assailed the forensic report and related electronic documents, describing them as “nothing more than legal conclusions premised on false, erroneous assumptions,” and saying no witness had confirmed the claims.

“The so-called forensic report itself and alleged related electronic documents are further inadmissible, as they violate the absolute confidentiality provision under the Anti-Money Laundering Act,” the comment said.
Under the impeachment rules, the prosecution has 10 days to respond to the defense's comment.
Trial suspension
The impeachment trial is currently suspended to give way to Senate committee deliberations on the proposed 2027 national budget.
The Senate impeachment court is scheduled to reconvene on Nov. 9 at 10 a.m.

Following the decision to drop three Articles of Impeachment, the prosecution will pursue only Article II, which accuses Duterte of failing to fully declare her assets and divest from business interests, raising questions about her unexplained wealth.

Defense lead counsel Sheila Sison earlier said the move would not affect the defense panel's presentation of evidence, stressing that Duterte should still be allowed to address allegations already presented before the impeachment court.— MCG, GMA News
